items.title: How I reverse engineered a commercial spatial audio effect
items.summary: Article URL: http://epestr.com/blog/reverse-engineering-a-commercial-spatial-audio-effect/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50044272 Points: 33 # Comments: 12
items.content:
Back while I was using a different OS, I used a program which processed the audio being played in real time and made it sound much better. It made the sound feel farther away and a bit lighter to hear, while carrying the relevant information. I'd always wanted a similar program which was equally simple to use for Linux, and decided to write one.

Listen with headphones. The excerpt is from P.I.M.P. by Bacao Rhythm & Steel Band [0] .

The processed version sounds farther from the ears and feels less "on the ear" making it feel less "blocked" after listening to music for a while.

Since I was writing for Linux, my base stack was PipeWire [1] . I had no prior audio experience, so I began by using an LLM as a sounding board while experimenting with standard audio filters and psychoacoustic techniques.

Somewhere along the way I learnt about HRTFs, which describe how sound arriving from a particular direction reaches the ears, depending on the direction and geometry of the listener. I tried the MIT KEMAR database [2] first and thought it sounded awful, because it had been recorded in an anechoic chamber, so there were no room echoes, which were a desirable psychoacoustic effect here. The result sounded cheap and more inwards to the ear. Later I found the SADIE II database [3] , which also came with room responses, and that sounded much closer to what I remembered.

But this approach soon showed its limits. The LLM began talking about things like "perceptual envelopment", "late-field decorrelation", "spectral diffusion" and "diffuse spatial energy". [1] [1] Gemini was particularly good at this. It was also the only one with a free student program. While I could hear that something was wrong, those descriptions didn't point to anything I could understand or use to improve the effect.

I left the project dead for a while with no obvious direction to proceed with.

Much later, I had a different idea. Instead of trying to discover the exact parameters or techniques and algorithms the program used internally, I could study the behaviour of the filter itself.

This seems obvious in retrospect, but I did not have a copy of the program. I could only experiment on a friend's laptop, so I could not keep changing my implementation and comparing it with the reference whenever I wanted.

I began reading Signalsmith [4] and some blogs by audio engineers to build enough intuition to know what I should measure, and soon realised that I didn't need to keep using the program to capture its impulse responses and other measurable features. I generated an audio file on Linux, got my friend's laptop for a while, played the generated file through the program and recorded the output.

The question became what I should put into that file so it could capture the relevant details which differentiated the program without having to re-record features or filters.

The first useful thing I found was impulse-response measurement.

If I pass a file containing a single nonzero sample through the filter, everything which appears after it in the recording would've been added by the filter. Features such as the extent of its decay over time, the shape of the decay and the phase delays associated with it would be present in the output. Playing the impulse in the right channel allows extracting both outputs' responses to sound played on the right, and likewise for the left.

If the response to one impulse is $h$, then the response to an impulse at position $k$ is the same $h$ shifted to $k$ and scaled by $x[k]$. Adding all of those responses gives

This of course depends on the filter being a linear time-invariant filter [5] .

A louder impulse should produce the same response made proportionally louder:

Two inputs played together should produce the sum of what each input produces separately:

And playing the same input later should produce the same response later.

Given I was sending one file to have it recorded through every mode, I added impulses at different amplitudes to check for level-dependent processing, and played the same impulse in both channels, then with the right channel inverted. The outputs should match the isolated responses added together in the first case and subtracted in the second, checking the conditions above. I also left enough silence between them for the response to finish before the next impulse.

While reading about this, I noticed that papers on measurement tended to use sine sweeps rather than impulses [6] . [2] [2] An impulse already contained every frequency, but having only one sample meant there was little energy at each frequency, so a long sweep would make the response easier to distinguish from recording noise.

This would work for most of the range, but if $X(f)$ was close to zero, dividing recording noise by it would make a rather impressive filter which had little to do with the program. This could be avoided with a regularized version.

With enough input energy this would approximately be the same division, while $\lambda$ would limit the result elsewhere. The complex values also retain the phase, which was required given sound sent to one channel could appear in the other with a delay.

The sweep gave another measurement to compare with the impulse, but it also took much longer to play, during which the program could change its behaviour. I added steady tones at different frequencies and amplitudes, and longer tones going from quiet to loud and back, to see whether the gain changed and how long it took to do so.

And I kept a section of noise aside, to test whether the extracted filter could reproduce its recorded output afterwards.

Given recording and playback were started manually, the recording first needed an offset. I had put evenly spaced clicks near the start, which I initially tried finding by correlating the recording with the original clicks. Since the filter could spread each click over time, I summed the squared samples over a window $W$ to estimate the energy around it instead,

I applied the same offset to both channels so the delay between them was retained.

For the main surround setting, the scaled impulses were nearly identical, the combined inputs matched the sum of their separate responses, and the multitone produced almost no new frequencies. To compare the reconstructed output with the recording, I used

where $y$ was the recorded output and $\hat y$ the output produced by the extracted filter. Given the identical repeated sections already differed slightly, I compared the model's error with that difference,

The volume-reducing mode changed its gain with amplitude and took time to restore it, while another spatial mode changed between repeats, so neither could be reproduced with a fixed convolution filter.

Recording both output channels for an impulse in each input channel gave me the four filters.

Sound also appeared in the opposite channel, quieter and slightly delayed, followed by a long tail. Together these contained the out-of-head effect I had been trying to make earlier.

To decide how much of this response to keep, I tried increasingly long filters against the noise section,

and kept the full response, which predicted the noise more accurately than the shorter versions. The response extracted from the sweep also agreed over the range where it had enough input energy.

Loading the four responses into Saq [7] gave me the placement I had been trying to reproduce by hand.

You can try the result here. Choose your own local audio file or capture a tab (when not in a Firefox browser [8] ), then click the square surround icon to toggle the effect.

items.title: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says
items.summary: The PM was speaking after violent attacks at Polish schools this week left one dead and others injured.
items.content:
Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.

The attacks have left one woman dead and others injured, including children.

"These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity," Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with security services.

Police have arrested 117 people across the country for possession knives or other weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students, after searching tens of thousands of schools.

A woman was arrested on Saturday after injuring three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw.

It came a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker.

"We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said on Sunday.

"In the past years and months, we have noted - globally and in Poland - a rise in the fascination with violence," he added.

The prime minister said the attacks were acts of "nihilistic violence" associated with the extreme right.

"Some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment," he said, adding that police had noticed a rise in online searches of Nazi content as well as of "mass killers who have become idols online".

On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.

A day later, the 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".

Thousands of Polish ‌police officers visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after the stabbings sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of more attacks stemming from a supposed online challenge.

Meanwhile, Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a spokesperson said.

A special services spokesman said officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".

Woman injures three people in third Poland school knife attack in a week

Caretaker killed and two teachers injured in knife attack at Poland school

items.title: Oltre 700 morti sul lavoro. Anmil, 'introdurre il reato di omicidio'
items.summary: Mattarella nella Giornata per la sicurezza: 'Servono prevenzione e formazione adeguata'
items.content:
Oltre 700 morti sul lavoro da gennaio ad oggi , quasi 405 denunce di infortuni e poco meno di 75.000 di malattia professionale. Sono i numeri drammatici che l'Anmil , l'associazione fra lavoratori mutilati e invalidi del lavoro, snocciola sulla base dei recenti dati dell'Inail, evidenziando che - nonostante gli sforzi e una giustizia spesso "di facciata" - il fenomeno continua ad avere in Italia tutte le caratteristiche di un'emergenza.

In occasione della 76/a Giornata nazionale per le vittime degli incidenti sul lavoro è del resto anche il presidente della Repubblica Sergio Mattarella a ricordare come la tutela della salute e della sicurezza nei luoghi di lavoro trovi "il suo fondamento nei principi della Costituzione. Da essi - spiega il capo dello Stato - discende un dovere concreto: intervenire sui rischi prima che si traducano in incidenti, attraverso una prevenzione efficace, una formazione adeguata e misure di protezione capaci di ottimizzare, a questo scopo, i cambiamenti tecnologici e organizzativi del lavoro".

Una linea condivisa dalla ministra del Lavoro, Marina Calderone . "La prevenzione rappresenta la prima e più importante forma di tutela della vita e della dignità delle persone. La sicurezza sul lavoro si costruisce intervenendo prima che si verifichi un incidente, prima che un rischio si trasformi in una tragedia". Scegliendo Longarone, in ricordo del disastro del Vajont, come sede nazionale per le celebrazioni che si svolgono su tutto il territorio italiano, l'Anmil ribadisce quindi la sua richiesta: istituire il reato autonomo di 'omicidio sul lavoro' nell'ordinamento giuridico italiano.

"Non si tratta di giustizialismo, - afferma il presidente Amedeo Bozzer , ricordando la proposta di legge attualmente all'esame della Commissione Giustizia della Camera - bensì di inaugurare una nuova era di giustizia sociale che merita basi solide volte a ritrovare la perduta fiducia nella capacità dello Stato di tutelare la sicurezza dei lavoratori". Per restituire dignità alla salute e sicurezza dei lavoratori l'associazione pensa anche all'istituzione di una Procura Nazionale del Lavoro, capace di accentrare e uniformare le indagini in materia superando la frammentazione territoriale e "guidata da una squadra di magistrati esperti della vastità tematica che la sicurezza del lavoro abbraccia. Una Procura che faccia finalmente scuola, reale e non solo di facciata", spiega Bozzer.

items.title: Il Papa e il nodulo polmonare, ecco come si diagnostica e quando si interviene
items.summary: L'esperto: 'Non equivale a diagnosi di tumore. Tecniche mininvasive e percorsi di cura'
items.content:
"La presenza di un nodulo polmonare richiede una valutazione medica attenta, ma non deve essere automaticamente associato a una patologia maligna e non permette, da sola, di formulare una diagnosi di tumore. Senza informazioni cliniche non è possibile stabilire la natura di una specifica lesione, che può avere diverse origini e diversi percorsi di cura". A fare il punto, dopo l'annuncio di Papa Leone XIV, è Federico Venuta, ordinario di Chirurgia toracica all'Università La Sapienza e direttore dell'Unità di Chirurgia toracica al Policlinico Umberto I di Roma.

Un nodulo polmonare è un'opacità isolata, di forma rotonda simile a una piccola moneta con un diametro inferiore ai 3 centimetri, che appare più densa rispetto al tessuto circostante nelle immagini radiologiche. "La sua individuazione è relativamente frequente e avviene spesso in maniera occasionale, durante esami eseguiti per altri motivi. Le cause possono essere diverse: accanto alle lesioni tumorali - spiega Venuta - ci sono condizioni benigne, come cicatrici di vecchie infezioni, piccoli granulomi infiammatori o alterazioni autoimmuni. In base alle circostanze in cui viene individuato il nodulo e alle sue caratteristiche, nonché alle caratteristiche del paziente (come l'abitudine al fumo) il medico può richiedere una tomografia computerizzata (la cosiddetta Tac) del torace per definirne grandezza, forma e struttura".

I noduli di dimensioni molto ridotte presentano un rischio inferiore di malignità: al di sotto dei 6 millimetri, infatti, può essere sufficiente rimandare a un controllo radiologico a distanza di qualche mese per assicurarsi che non cresca. Se il nodulo è più grande o presenta margini irregolari, il percorso diagnostico può prevedere una Pet. La fase successiva è quella della biopsia, per prelevare un campione di cellule o tessuto da analizzare o per rimuovere il nodulo con intervento chirurgico, nel caso in cui la biopsia non sia praticabile. Se dall'esame istologico la lesione risulta benigna, non sono necessari trattamenti. Se viene identificato un tumore primitivo del polmone in fase iniziale, in genere l'asportazione chirurgia è sufficiente. Quando invece emergono ulteriori elementi di rischio - prosegue l'esperto - si valutano trattamenti oncologici di tipo farmacologico o radioterapico".

Un precedente noto è quello di re Juan Carlos di Spagna, che nel 2019 all'età di 72 anni, si è sottoposto a un intervento al polmone per un nodulo che risultò benigno. "Un caso che ricorda come il riscontro di una lesione polmonare non equivalga a una diagnosi di tumore maligno". Naturalmente, ogni situazione clinica è diversa e non è possibile stabilire analogie con il caso di Papa Leone in assenza di informazioni mediche specifiche. Quel che è certo è che il pontefice dovrà operarsi la prossima settimana, ma il professor Venuta rassicura: "Negli ultimi anni la chirurgia toracica ha compiuto importanti progressi grazie alle tecniche mininvasive, che permettono di intervenire con incisioni ridotte e favorire un rapido recupero. I tempi di degenza sono in genere di 5-7 giorni".

"Seguiamo con partecipe attenzione la notizia appena annunciata dal Santo Padre e gli esprimiamo tutta la nostra vicinanza. Ci uniamo nella preghiera e gli rivolgiamo i più affettuosi auguri per l'intervento e per una pronta ripresa". Così il presidente della Federazione nazionale degli Ordini dei medici chirurghi e degli odontoiatri ( Fnomceo ), Filippo Anelli, dopo l'annuncio del Papa di un intervento programmato nei prossimi giorni per rimuovere un nodulo al polmone, in fase iniziale e ben localizzato.

"Le sue parole - continua Anelli - esprimono fiducia nei medici e nelle loro indicazioni, un sentimento che accogliamo con gratitudine e senso di responsabilità. Affidarsi a chi ci cura significa poter contare sulla competenza, sull'ascolto e su una relazione umana che accompagna ogni scelta, soprattutto nei momenti di maggiore fragilità". "Il nostro pensiero - aggiunge - va anche ai colleghi e a tutti i professionisti sanitari che si prenderanno cura di lui. A loro rivolgiamo un messaggio di sostegno e riconoscenza per il compito che sono chiamati a svolgere".

Anche chirurghi italiani, riuniti a Roma per la cerimonia inaugurale del 128/mo Congresso Nazionale della Società Italiana di Chirurgia (Sic) , si stringono con affetto attorno a Prevost. "A nome di tutta la comunità chirurgica, la Società italiana di chirurgia rivolge al Santo Padre un pensiero di affetto e di vicinanza in vista dell'intervento, con l'auspicio di poterlo presto rivedere impegnato nella sua missione. La chirurgia italiana, per competenza ed esperienza, è riconosciuta tra le migliori al mondo, e i chirurghi riuniti al congresso guardano con piena fiducia al lavoro dei colleghi che si prenderanno cura del Pontefice", dichiara Ludovico Docimo, presidente della società scientifica.

items.title: Ukraine strikes Yandex data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
items.summary: It is the third time this week that Ukraine has targeted Russian tech giant Yandex, forcing the company to suspend its operations.
items.content:
Yandex has been forced to pause its operations at a data centre near Moscow after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike - the third attack on the Russian tech giant's sites this week.

The company - dubbed "Russia's Google" - said no one was injured at the centre in Vladimir, east of the capital, but some of its services were unavailable to users.

Earlier this week, Yandex said it was struggling to maintain its services after two of its five data centres were hit in Ukrainian strikes.

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between them continues in its fifth year following Russia's full-scale invasion.

Kyiv said it was targeting places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the attacks could force Russia to divert its resources to repair the damage at Yandex.

Sunday's attack came hours after US President Donald Trump warned that Ukraine should "damn well stop" attacking Russia's oil refineries so Moscow could release more diesel to the global market - a deal that has drawn criticism from Europe and sparked a diplomatic row with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.

'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal

Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices

Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said it was working to restore connectivity.

The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing problems for some of its services, such as its AI chatbot and smart home devices.

The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said at the time that its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.

Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued through the weekend.

The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.

On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed.

Russia has previously also struck Ukrainian data centres, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad.

items.title: I'm sorry, but you still have to think
items.summary: Article URL: https://itsallaboutthebit.com/i-am-sorry-but-you-still-have-to-think/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50043689 Points: 112 # Comments: 37
items.content:
DHH, the creator of the Ruby on Rails framework, decided to rewrite Campfire Once from Ruby on Rails to Rust. Or rather ask a clanker to do it for him, as he can't stand reading or writing the Rust code himself. After that he added rewrites in other languages , like Elixir and Go.

This is very interesting to me, as it's a very good insight into the results of someone using AI agents without reading the code. In this case, that someone has also a lot of prior programming experience. And the results are... well, not very encouraging if you are hoping you can stop reading the code, or stop thinking altogether anytime soon. There are multiple problems with the rewrites, but let's start with non-functional differences cause they nicely show something that a lot of people seem to not realize: if your prompt is not specific enough, many decisions are a coin flip. This is because a whole lot of questions don't have a single correct answer. Do we want to keep backwards compatibility? Do we care more about latency or throughput? How much memory can the system use under load? Is loosing new content notifications after a crash acceptable? You may not care about them, or at least some of them, but they will be implicitly answered when an LLM implements what you think you want.

If you look into the rewrites closer, you will quickly see that they treat backwards compatibility and other constraints differently. The Rust version doesn't maintain 100% backwards compatibility, for example it drops the CSRF token so that caching is easier. It also dropped Redis in favour of in-process queues, for example for notifications. Elixir rewrite is much closer to the Rails original. This already makes the comparison pretty much useless, as these differences are language independent. It's not like a clanker heard "rewrite in Elixir" and chose to keep 100% backwards compatibility because of the language that has been used. But it gets even better!

If you looked at the code, and yeah, I know, we should not be reading code anymore, you would quickly notice a lot of the things are not great. For example, I've seen people complaining that Elixir's version got a single process sequentially processing all of the SQL queries, even if these were reads that could be running concurrently. That's a fair complaint, but DHH seems to think it's not the best look for Elixir that the clanker couldn't write performant code. Not sure if I agree when I look at the Rust version. Cause in the Rust version some of the database operations are not async, which in some cases may be worse. You see, in Rust, when using an async runtime, the scheduling is not preemptive, but rather cooperative. If a task doesn't yield, no other task can run on the same worker thread. What this means in practice, is that the time spent in the task should be as short as possible. For example, when you run an SQL query that takes 100ms, you don't want all the other tasks to wait as the task issuing the query is waiting anyway. Thus, you should ideally use an async I/O operation that yields to the runtime while waiting for a response from the database. In the Rust rewrite some queries run on worker threads, but some run as blocking operations in async tasks. Same with locks. When using an async runtime, the safest bet is to use async locks like tokio::sync::Mutex . It's fine to use a non-async version if you're sure that the lock is held for a very short time, but if you hold a sync lock for 10ms, all the tasks on the same thread wait for it, while the blocking task itself is not doing any work. Thus, I regret to inform you, that no, coding is not likely "solved", and you still need to know what you're doing.

Going further, it turned out that slop benchmarks are also, well, slop, as they only measure throughput, disregarding other properties of the system. For example, Zach Daniels measured new post notifications delivery rate under load , and discovered a 1% successful delivery rate in the Rust version under heavy load. Not a great look. Benchmarks are hard. But even the improved benchmark may not be actually testing what you want to test, depending on the characteristics of your system. You see, when you test a system you may want to emphasize different properties under load. Both DHH's and Zach's benchmarks were closed-loop benchmarks, so they were testing "how many requests can the system handle in a specific amount of time?". The test was using N clients, each sending a new message as soon as it gets a response for the previous one. In many cases, though, the increased load on the system may come from a big number of users performing an action at the same time, who will not wait for other users to finish their actions. In this case you would prefer constant arrival rate , ie. you want to send requests at a constant rate rather than making the rate depend on how fast the system can respond. If you want to check how reliable the events delivery is, you would ideally want to compare the same number of events. Here, if you look at the results, it shows that Rust delivered 1% of notifications out of 6-7k, whereas Elixir delivered 100% of notifications out of ~1.7k. What it shows is that the Elixir version handles backpressure better, but this only holds as long as the number of requests don't overload the system.

But let's leave benchmarks just for a moment and talk about trade-offs, cause programming is all about trade-offs. Sure, there are situations where a tool or a solution is clearly better, without any downsides, but it's quite rare, especially when you get to complex systems that have to be reliable. I've seen quite a lot of people from the Elixir community coming to various conclusions after they've seen the 1% delivery rate of the Rust version, without really trying to understand why it happens. The general consensus? Elixir is just better at concurrency! In Rust the scheduler is cooperative, how can you even live like this? I like Elixir, and I've successfully used it in production, but it's not a silver bullet. Yes, Elixir (or other BEAM based languages) are very good at concurrency, and admittedly writing concurrent code in Elixir is, in general, easier than in Rust, but it comes at a cost of not having low level control, higher memory usage, and oftentimes, speed. There is a reason why rustler exists. And proclaiming language's superiority based on a single metric without knowing the root cause, may be misleading.

Remember how I mentioned the closed-loop stress test shows just one of the properties of the system as Rust processed ~4 times more requests and thus had to handle more events sent to the client through a WebSocket? I've rerun the test with constant delivery rate using the DHH's Rust version and Zach's Elixir version with various fixes. At 100 POSTs/s the clients received ~14% events in Rust. In Elixir it was ~60%. Still better, right? Not so fast! At this traffic level Rust didn't have any HTTP errors. Elixir timed out on ~23% of HTTP POST requests. And what about latency? The worst event delivery latency was close to 180s. In Rust when the deliveries are lagging, clients get disconnected. On reconnect, a browser client would fetch the latest messages, which largely invalidates the need for the missed events. What do you think is better UX: the client silently reconnecting in the background and fetching the new updates, or waiting for an update about a new message for 3 minutes? Which just shows that, again, a single metric doesn't tell the whole story.

Getting back to trade-offs. Do you know why the Rust version drops so many messages under heavy load? It uses tokio::sync::broadcast channel to broadcast events to connected clients. An event informing about a new chat message may need to be sent to multiple connections, so that makes total sense. One of the properties of the broadcast channel is that it's bounded by a set capacity. If a receiver can't handle the messages fast enough, the receiver will get a RecvError::Lagged error (refer to the docs to learn more about lagging ). The broadcast capacity in the Rust rewrite was set to 256. In Elixir, the GenServer process is handling events delivery and by default GenServer mailboxes don't have a limit. A single line change in Rust:

increases the delivery rate at 100 req/s from ~14% to ~90%. It's better than Elixir now, isn't it? Not really. I think that this version is actually worse because in this case it's better to fail fast and force the client to reconnect rather than handle things extremely slowly. You know what else changed after raising the capacity? The pMAX event delivery latency went up from 11s to >130s, similarly to how Elixir behaved, which I think is strictly worse than disconnecting the lagging clients. If you ask me, even 11s is too long and if the receiver can't pass the event faster than that, it's better to drop the event. Which shows how important it is to set sensible constraints in the system, and that, in fact, Elixir isn't just automatically fixing all of the concurrency issues out of the box. Also, if you don't set bounds yourself, you will likely run into external limits. During the 100 req/s stress test the Elixir version reached 1.8GB memory usage. Another thing to ponder on: is it better to drop some messages or get OOM killed? Trade-offs all the way. Elixir is great, but it won't magically solve all of your problems. No matter the language you're using, you have to think about failure modes and trade-offs.

items.title: Documents add to evidence in climate deception case against ExxonMobil
items.summary: Article URL: https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07102026/exxonmobil-climate-deception-new-evidence/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50043682 Points: 335 # Comments: 173
items.content:
If there was a year the world began waking up to climate change, it might have been 1988. That June, the NASA climatologist James Hansen testified to Congress that the climate was warming and would continue to do so as long as humans pumped fossil fuel pollution into the atmosphere. Months later, the United Nations established the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

And, just weeks before the U.N. vote, Frank Sprow of Exxon’s corporate research department warned his colleagues in an internal memo , “If a worldwide consensus emerges that action is needed to mitigate against Greenhouse gas effects, substantial negative impacts on Exxon could occur.”

Sprow’s memo is part of a batch of previously undisclosed documents released earlier this year without fanfare as part of an ongoing lawsuit Massachusetts filed against ExxonMobil in 2019. While the memo was quoted in a 2023 article by The Wall Street Journal , it has not been published in full. Several other documents included in the filings are being reported on here for the first time, including more recent statements from Exxon scientists challenging the company’s climate-solution claims about its work on biofuels and carbon capture and storage.

While the documents align with hundreds of confidential files that have previously come to light through reporting by Inside Climate News and other news organizations, as well as lawsuits and other sources, experts say they provide new details on internal deliberations at Exxon from the 1980s to the 2010s.

The release of the documents comes at a pivotal time for the oil industry and for efforts to hold it accountable for its role fueling climate change. This week, the U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments from Exxon and oil producer Suncor Energy that a lawsuit filed by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, should be halted. The outcome of that decision could decide whether more than two dozen other claims against oil companies proceed.

Aaron Regunberg, director of climate accountability at the advocacy group Public Citizen, said the documents from the Massachusetts case underscore why Exxon and other companies are fighting to block the lawsuits from even proceeding to the discovery phase.

“They are really scared of the public finding out about this reality,” Regunberg said of oil companies. The Massachusetts filings, he said, suggest “that we have seen just a sliver of the evidence that they actually have that they’ve spent decades knowingly deceiving the public about this crisis. How many more reports are they sitting on?”

Most of the lawsuits assert that oil companies should help pay the escalating costs being imposed on the public by climate-fueled extreme weather because they knew the risks their products posed but worked to publicly question climate science and stymie efforts to curb emissions. Those costs have surged, topping $100 billion in the U.S. in four of the last five years. Exxon, meanwhile, reported nearly $19 billion in earnings over the first six months of this year alone.

Exxon did not respond to requests for comment, but it has denied misleading the public or investors about climate change. In its annual securities filing, the company said of the lawsuits, “We believe the legal and factual theories set forth in these proceedings are meritless and represent an inappropriate attempt to use the court system to usurp the proper role of policymakers in addressing the societal challenges of climate change.”

The case brought by the Massachusetts attorney general’s office in state court is slightly different from others, arguing that the company deceived the state’s consumers and investors into thinking it was taking action to limit warming when those efforts were more about public relations than real action. The state is seeking fines and an injunction blocking Exxon’s allegedly deceptive practices.

The new documents, filed as part of a dispute over whether Exxon should be forced to hand over more files and testimony, help lay out the state’s case.

Take biofuels. For years, Exxon ran a sustained public relations campaign touting its research into using algae to make fuel, which it said could be a sustainable alternative to petroleum.

In March, The Wall Street Journal reported on internal documents that showed Exxon’s scientists told executives the company’s targets were not feasible. The new disclosures in the Massachusetts case add to the evidence with excerpts from a deposition by an Exxon scientist who worked on the program.

Asked whether a 2018 press release , which said Exxon anticipated “10,000 barrels of algae biofuel per day could be produced by 2025,” was misleading, the scientist said “yes,” adding, “All the clauses in there are patently false.”

The scientist testified that the 10,000-barrel-per-day target was “completely impossible to achieve,” and that he told this to others at the company before the press release was issued.

In another instance, the scientist said a research development on algae that Exxon publicly claimed as a breakthrough was, in fact, “ a dead end .”

Exxon later dropped its research into algae biofuels but has continued to promote carbon capture and storage as a climate solution. The documents include some statements which, according to the attorney general’s office, show Exxon knew that technology was also unlikely to present a scalable solution to cutting emissions.

A 2014 presentation on Exxon’s carbon capture portfolio included a slide listing challenges to reaching commercial scale. It noted widespread deployment would require a “massive investment” and an eventual storage rate “comparable to current oil and gas production.” It said costs were high and there were no market-based incentives.

Three years later, a different Exxon scientist was asked by a colleague to record an advertisement for the technology. He noted that the company was calling itself a leader in carbon capture but said he was “not a big fan” of the claim. At the time, Exxon’s carbon capture operations were largely restricted to gas processing plants that stripped the climate pollutant out of methane and injected it into oil or gas fields. That technology, he said, “has nothing to do” with the type of carbon capture that Exxon and others were promoting for power plants and industrial facilities.

That scientist later appeared in an ad promoting research he was conducting on carbon capture without any claim that Exxon was a leader in the technology.

Another presentation from 2017 appears to show the advertisements for algae and carbon capture were among the company’s highest performing, calling them “All-Around Winners.”

In 2021, Exxon was still promoting its work in carbon capture. An internal presentation about an advertising campaign targeting political and financial leaders said its objective was to get people to “believe ExxonMobil is committed to helping solve climate change” and to proving the company and carbon capture and storage “play an indispensable role in facilitating the transition to a lower carbon energy system.”

Under a header of “what we’re doing,” the presentation listed a proposed hub for carbon capture in Houston that Exxon no longer promotes.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

While the Massachusetts case focuses on these more recent campaigns, the filings include earlier records that serve as concise roadmaps for what would become Exxon’s climate strategy in the following decades, said Geoffrey Supran, an associate professor of environmental science and policy at the University of Miami. He has published studies comparing Exxon’s public statements with its internal documents and is a consulting expert on some climate-related legal actions.

It was November 1988, five months after Hansen’s congressional testimony, when Sprow filed his draft memo .

With the threat of climate action looming, he wrote, the company’s research and development on “Greenhouse” should have two primary goals: “Protect the value of our resources (oil, gas, coal),” and “Preserve Exxon’s business options.”

Sprow then laid out an agenda for how to achieve those ends.

With modeling critical to climate science, he wrote, “it could be considered important to be at the forefront of this modeling effort.” Sprow proposed “supporting a person on staff at one of the leading modeling centers (e.g. Princeton) or by sending one of our people to work in such a center.”

Sprow also recommended monitoring alternative energy technologies, including nuclear, solar and biofuels, to understand their viability as alternatives to fossil fuels or, eventually, for possible business development. Finally, he added, Exxon could look for “a research breakthrough” in one of these areas that would align with the company’s business.

Sprow did not respond to requests for comment from Inside Climate News, but he told The Wall Street Journal that his memo was adopted as corporate policy.

items.title: F1: Verstappen vince a Singapore davanti a Leclerc, Kimi terzo
items.summary: Nuovo passo in avanti di Antonelli verso il mondiale piloti
items.content:
"Davvero? Sicuro?". Grondante di sudore dopo 62 giri nell'inferno umido di Marina Bay, Kimi Antonelli aveva ancora voglia di fare il finto tonto e ha risposto così alla domanda se fosse consapevole di poter diventare campione del mondo già alla prossima gara, il Gp degli Usa. Un atteggiamento che conferma il carattere spigliato del ventenne bolognese, quasi opposto alla cattiveria agonistica del vincente innato che anche stavolta ha messo in pista per superare nel finale Lando Norris e ottenere nel Gp di Singapore un terzo posto che vale oro alle spalle del vincitore, Max Verstappen, e di Charles Leclerc, secondo. Grazie ai 15 punti, ed al nono posto di George Russell, ora Antonelli ha sul compagno di squadra un vantaggio di 102 punti e di 111 su Lewis Hamilton.

Per laurearsi campione tra due settimane dovrebbe vincere ad Austin, con Russell al massimo nono al traguardo ed Hamilton al massimo quinto . Antonelli, come si è capito, non fa tanti calcoli e ha promesso che in Usa l'unica sua preoccupazione sarà "fare il miglior weekend possibile per completare l'opera". "Oggi la gara è stata molto dura ma son davvero contento del risultato - ha sottolineato -. Sono riuscito a sfruttare la lotta tra Norris ed Hamilton e sono molto felice di averli superati entrambi per salire sul podio ".

Altrettanto soddisfatto, al momento della premiazione, è apparso Verstappen, che è riuscito ad aggiungere al suo palmares una delle poche gare che mancavano. Una Red Bull tornata degna del suo pilota di punta gli ha permesso di fare en plein , ottenendo la seconda vittoria stagionale consecutiva oltre al successo nella Sprint e doppia pole position. Al verde, l'olandese ha rintuzzato con molta decisione un deciso attacco di Leclerc, che partiva al suo fianco , e da quel momento ha condotto la gara alla sua maniera, tagliando il traguardo con oltre sette secondi di vantaggio sulla Ferrari del monegasco.

"Ci è voluto un po', ma penso che questa gara sia stata molto bella - ha commentato dopo aver coronato con la vittoria la 250/a gara in carriera -. Speriamo di poterci divertire ancora". Un Verstappen così darà una bella scossa al finale di una stagione già decisa, ponendo nuove sfide anche ad una Ferrari in ripresa. Leclerc ha saputo difendere il secondo posto gestendo bene la varie fasi di gara, mentre Lewis Hamilton ha pagato cara una scelta sbagliata fatta in regime di virtual safety car al 39/o giro : la Scuderia ha richiamato entrambi ai box per un secondo pit ma mentre Leclerc ha calzato gomme soft nuove, il britannico che era secondo ha deciso di continuare con le soft ormai usurate e così è stato superato da Leclerc, Antonelli, Lando Norris e Oscar Piastri, terminando al sesto posto . "Scusate ragazzi, vi ho deluso con quella strategia - ha ammesso al team radio -. È stata una mia decisione e ci ha fatto perdere punti preziosi. Cercherò di rifarmi nella prossima gara".

Il britannico dopo la gara ha accusato un lieve malore - ha fatto sapere il team - e la Fia gli ha permesso di non fare la conferenza stampa post-gara. Il team principal, Fred Vasseur, ha detto che il pluricampione del mondo "ha sbagliato a non rientrare. Poteva conquistare il terzo posto . Ma non sono arrabbiato - ha aggiunto - in generale questo è stato un buon fine settimana. Dovremo parlarne con Lewis in modo che situazioni del genere non si ripetano" . Leclerc ha spiegato di "non avere rimpianti per la gara, abbiamo fatto il massimo possibile. Siamo stati abbastanza forti all'inizio poi abbiamo iniziato a calare".

items.title: Pope Leo to have surgery after lump found on lung
items.summary: The 71-year-old pontiff said the nodule was identified "at a very early stage".
items.content:
Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up.

"The doctors found an early, well-localised nodule on my lung," he told the public during his weekly Sunday prayers in St Peter's Square in Rome.

The 71-year-old said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation, while reassuring pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage".

The pontiff's admission that he would need surgery comes nearly a year-and-a-half after he succeeded the late Pope Francis, who also experienced issues with his lungs that required hospital treatment.

Leo concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers.

Holy See Press Office spokesman Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week".

He added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover.

Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome.

The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today.

Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her "personal solidarity" with the Pope as he "faces the ordeal ahead in the coming days".

Her sentiments were echoed by Italian President Sergio Mattarella, who offered his "sincerest wishes for a peaceful recovery and a speedy and full return to health".

Isaac Herzog, the president of Israel, also wished the pontiff "a full and speedy recovery".

The Pope, born Robert Francis Prevost, is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter – the first US citizen to do so.

He was ordained in 1982 and spent years as a missionary in Peru, where he is remembered as a figure who worked with marginalised communities.

During Sunday's service, the Pope confirmed his upcoming visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November will still go ahead.

The Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla, said preparations for his tour will continue with "greater enthusiasm" as he called for prayers for his recovery.

A lung nodule is a small lump of tissue that is usually detected following an X-ray or CT scan of the chest, according to the NHS.

items.title: Il caso Reggio Children, la comunità ebraica di Milano: 'Metodi da Terzo Reich, l'amministrazione si dimetta'
items.summary: La replica del sindaco Massari: 'L'antisemitismo non è la nostra storia'
items.content:
"I metodi e il clima instaurati da certi Comuni emiliani mi ricordano molto quelli di Goebbels e quanto scriveva il gerarca fascista Roberto Farinacci: 'ebrei razza immonda da seppellire in quanto tali'. Non si può chiedere a un cittadino americano, a un docente, a un ebreo, di rispondere come ebreo, in quanto tale. È la negazione totale dell'inclusione che a parole si dice di voler promuovere. È antisemitismo. Chiedo che l'Amministrazione comunale di Reggio Emilia si dimetta". Lo afferma Walker Meghnagi, presidente della Comunità ebraica di Milano , dopo le polemiche sul caso delle delegazioni ebraiche in visita al Reggio Children .

"Al Comune di Reggio Emilia - afferma - si promuovono progetti sull'inclusione e sui valori democratici, si invitano docenti americani di religione ebraica per attività didattiche e di dialogo, e poi si pretende di imporre loro dittatorialmente di prendere posizione su una vicenda politica, solo ed esclusivamente perché per il Comune di Reggio Emilia questi insegnanti appartengono alla 'razza ebraica'. È un principio di schedatura su base razziale". La richiesta di dimissioni, motiva Meghnagi, è "per il metodo indegno utilizzato e per l'enorme danno di immagine provocato all'Italia, visto che la notizia campeggia ormai in tutti i telegiornali americani e sta facendo il giro del mondo". L'Italia, conclude, "non può permettersi di passare per un Paese che discrimina gli ebrei in quanto ebrei".

A stretto giro arriva la replica del sindaco, Marco Massari . "Le dichiarazioni del presidente della Comunità ebraica di Milano, Walker Meghnagi, ci sorprendono", dice. "Respingiamo con fermezza le accuse di antisemitismo rivolte al Comune di Reggio Emilia, che non corrispondono in alcun modo ai nostri valori, alla nostra storia e alle ragioni del nostro impegno educativo. Ci auguriamo che queste parole siano frutto di informazioni non complete e che sia possibile chiarire ogni equivoco, senza sovrapporre al confronto educativo valutazioni di natura politica".

La bufera è nata dopo che la società Reggio Children, a capitale misto pubblico-privato, avrebbe chiesto ad insegnanti israeliani e americani che volevano partecipare a un programma sull'educazione della prima infanzia - in programma da domani al 16 ottobre - di sottoscrivere, in quanto ebrei, una dichiarazione di dissociazione dalle azioni del governo israeliano. Richiesta rifiutata dalla delegazione di insegnanti ebrei americani, che ha rinunciato alla visita in città.

items.title: Leone XIV, i messaggi dopo l’annuncio dell’intervento. Mattarella: “Il popolo italiano le è vicino”
items.summary: La vicinanza delle istituzioni e la preghiera della Chiesa dopo le parole del Papa all’Angelus. Meloni sottolinea la serenità del Pontefice, Zuppi gli assicura il sostegno delle comunità
items.content:
L’affetto degli italiani, le preghiere delle comunità cattoliche, gli auguri delle istituzioni. Dopo l’annuncio di Leone XIV , che al termine dell’Angelus ha comunicato di doversi sottoporre nei prossimi giorni a un intervento per rimuovere un nodulo polmonare, arrivano i messaggi di vicinanza al Pontefice. A colpire, nelle parole della presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni , è anche la serenità con cui il Papa ha condiviso la notizia con i fedeli.

Il presidente della Repubblica Sergio Mattarella gli ha inviato un messaggio facendosi interprete del sentimento del Paese. “Il Suo annuncio all’Angelus di oggi è stato accolto con partecipazione e commozione da tutto il popolo italiano”, scrive il capo dello Stato. In vista del ricovero, al Pontefice giunge “l’affettuoso pensiero degli italiani tutti”, al quale Mattarella unisce il proprio. Una vicinanza che, sottolinea, va oltre l’appartenenza religiosa: “Ella potrà contare, oltre che sulle preghiere dei fedeli cattolici, sul partecipe pensiero di innumerevoli persone, in Italia come da ogni parte del mondo, siano essi credenti o non credenti”. Il messaggio si conclude con l’augurio di “una serena convalescenza” e di un “pronto e completo ristabilimento”.

Meloni esprime la vicinanza personale e del governo “per la prova che è chiamato ad affrontare nei prossimi giorni”. E aggiunge: “La serenità e la tranquillità con cui ne ha parlato nell’Angelus di oggi ci rincuorano”. La premier si dice certa che il popolo italiano non farà mancare al Papa sostegno e affetto.

Gli auguri arrivano anche dai presidenti delle Camere. Ignazio La Russa auspica che l’intervento possa svolgersi nel migliore dei modi e rivolge, a nome proprio e del Senato,”un affettuoso augurio di pronta e completa guarigione”. Lorenzo Fontana assicura preghiere e vicinanza: “Lo accompagniamo in questi giorni con tutto il nostro affetto, sempre grati per il suo impegno costante e per le sue parole”.

Alla solidarietà delle istituzioni si unisce quella della Chiesa italiana. Il cardinale Matteo Zuppi , arcivescovo di Bologna e presidente della Cei, accoglie l’invito del Pontefice alla vicinanza spirituale e assicura il ricordo nelle celebrazioni e nei momenti di preghiera delle comunità. “Ringraziamo Papa Leone per la semplicità e la fiducia con cui ci ha reso partecipi di questa prova”, afferma. Poi si rivolge direttamente a Prevost: “Siamo una famiglia: Santo Padre, non è solo!”. Le Chiese in Italia, aggiunge, lo accompagnano con la preghiera e l’affetto perché l’intervento vada bene e possa affrontarlo con serenità e forza.

“Preghiamo per lui, così lui ci ha chiesto, così facciamo”, dice il cardinale Mario Grech , segretario generale del Sinodo dei vescovi. Davide Prosperi , presidente della Fraternità di Comunione e Liberazione, invita il movimento a recitare il Rosario, in comunità e in famiglia, per il Papa e per le sue intenzioni. Anche il Rinnovamento nello Spirito esprime solidarietà e auspica che Leone XIV possa ristabilirsi presto. I dipendenti laici del Vaticano, attraverso l’esecutivo della loro associazione, si uniscono nella preghiera per la sua salute e gli augurano di riprendere presto la missione pastorale.

Un applauso di solidarietà al Pontefice ha chiuso a Milano l’evento di Forza Italia “L’ottimismo della volontà”. A chiederlo è stato Antonio Tajani : “Siamo vicini a Papa Leone”. Il vicepremier e ministro degli Esteri aveva già scritto su X che tutti gli italiani si stringono attorno al Santo Padre, assicurando una preghiera “per la sua salute e per il suo magistero”. Matteo Salvini e la Lega esprimono affetto e auguri di pronta ripresa, accompagnando il Papa “con il pensiero e con la preghiera in questi giorni delicati”.

Maurizio Lupi , presidente di Noi Moderati, richiama il servizio del Pontefice alla Chiesa e all’umanità e il suo impegno per la pace e per i più fragili. La ministra Elisabetta Casellati auspica che possa riprendere al più presto il suo ministero, continuando a diffondere un messaggio di pace, speranza e fraternità. Francesco Battistoni , deputato di Forza Italia e segretario di Presidenza della Camera, definisce la serenità e la schiettezza dell’annuncio “un modello di grande forza morale”.

Da Roma, la città di cui il Papa è vescovo, il sindaco Roberto Gualtieri invia un caloroso augurio di pronta guarigione e il desiderio che Leone XIV possa tornare presto alle sue attività. Il presidente della Regione Lazio Francesco Rocca gli rivolge la vicinanza dell’intera comunità regionale: “A lui, così vicino alle sofferenze degli altri, va oggi il nostro abbraccio”.

items.title: A Nottingham il primo impegno pubblico congiunto in Gb per Harry e Meghan
items.summary: Giovedì visiteranno tre organizzazioni locali che aiutano i giovani
items.content:
Il principe Harry e sua moglie Meghan parteciperanno al loro primo impegno pubblico congiunto nel Regno Unito da quando si sono stabiliti nel Paese a fine agosto; lo hanno riferito diversi media britannici.

Secondo tali testate, tra cui il Sunday Times, giovedì il Duca e la Duchessa del Sussex si recheranno a Nottingham, la città dell'Inghilterra centrale dove fecero la loro prima apparizione pubblica insieme dopo l'annuncio del fidanzamento nel 2017.

A Nottingham, la coppia dovrebbe visitare tre organizzazioni locali che aiutano i giovani attraverso la musica, il cinema e lo sport, oltre a combattere la povertà, secondo quanto riportato dal 'Sunday Times'.

Citando una fonte vicina alla coppia, il giornale riferisce inoltre che il Duca e la Duchessa non saranno invitati al tradizionale raduno natalizio della famiglia reale presso la residenza di Carlo III a Sandringham (nell'Inghilterra orientale), ma trascorreranno le festività in California.

Dal loro ritorno nel Regno Unito con i due figli, Archie e Lilibet, dopo sei anni trascorsi negli Stati Uniti, Harry e Meghan hanno mantenuto un profilo relativamente riservato, sebbene il figlio minore di re Carlo III abbia partecipato a diversi impegni pubblici per organizzazioni benefiche di cui è patrono o sostenitore. Meghan, dal canto suo, prosegue l'attività del suo marchio di prodotti lifestyle.

items.title: The tilde in your PATH may not be your HOME
items.summary: Article URL: https://disconnect3d.pl//2026/10/02/dont-put-tilde-in-your-path/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50042425 Points: 154 # Comments: 87
items.content:
I was playing with the nono agent sandboxing tool and it greeted me with a warning: PATH entries the sandbox can write to: ~/.local/bin/ which looked suspicious.

will not expand the ~ (tilde) into the home path (or $HOME ) as the tilde to home expansion happens only in unquoted inputs, as also the bash documentation says :

If a word begins with an unquoted tilde character (‘~’), all of the characters up to the first unquoted slash (…) are considered a tilde-prefix. (…)

Bash checks each variable assignment for unquoted tilde-prefixes immediately following a ‘:’ or the first ‘=’, and performs tilde expansion in these cases. (…)

So instead of having /home/ /.local/bin/ added to PATH we end up with ./~/.local/bin/ added to PATH .

Note that the unquoted version export PATH=$PATH:~/.local/bin actually works in Bash and Zsh, because tilde expansion is also performed in variable assignments after = and after each : . But relying on that is fragile as for example, a whitespace will break the variable assignment.

As we can see, the kek binary was found and executed from ./~/.local/bin/ — the home directory was never involved.

If it prints anything, go fix your .bashrc / .zshrc / .profile and replace the ~ with $HOME :).

Btw, kudos to the nono tool for warning about this - even though the warning could be more verbose (PR incoming).

items.title: Valen's Memory Safety: A New Kind of Borrow Checking
items.summary: Article URL: https://verdagon.dev/blog/valen-group-borrowing Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50042362 Points: 90 # Comments: 40
items.content:
This post is about Valen 's new flexible borrow checker. Welcome!

You all know me, I love exploring new memory safety approaches and blending them together in weird ways.

It's part of my eternal quest to find the memory safety holy grail: something as powerful as Rust's borrow checking, yet something as simple and flexible as reference counting or garbage collection. 0 1

I've long suspected that to find the holy grail, we'd have to solve three memory-safety challenges:

Vague and arcane, I know! Further below I'll explain what that all means, and how Valen might have found a solution for them. 5

This post mainly focuses on the first piece: Valen's more relaxed borrow checker.

So in this post, I'll talk about what it is, what it can do, and how it works.

And, along the way, I'll explain some of the weirder tidbits, like:

Also, this article is gloriously long and has a lot of context, so I'll let you know when to skip ahead.

(This is just backstory that I love telling, feel free to skip this section !)

Valen's approach is built on the "Group Borrowing" proposal which was designed by my friend Nick Smith .

It's built around the core concept that the compiler remembers where a reference points to, (I'll explain this later) and it uses that information to check that programs are memory-safe.

The design's life had a rough start; it was almost buried in the flows of time. It was originally designed with Mojo in mind , but alas, despite my best efforts I couldn't convince the higher-ups that we should use it. 7 Group borrowing was dead before it had the chance to succeed.

But I knew it had massive potential, if it could just make it into the world somehow.

So we spent months sharpening the explanation and figuring out its benefits, and wrote a post 8 on it last year, hoping other languages would pick it up.

Most of these languages are circling the same sort of challenge: how to make a more flexible borrow checker.

For example, Valen wants to make a borrow checker that's flexible enough to work with reference counting and generational references, and Carbon wants to make a borrow checker flexible enough to work with C++ code.

This is difficult, because there's been a fundamental conflict between borrow checking and other approaches. It can be summed up like this: 13

You're probably thinking, "There's definitely no way to resolve this."

But group borrowing actually resolves the conflict, by relaxing "shared-xor-mutable" to "no use-after-free".

That was cryptic and won't make any sense, but it will later when I explain how group borrowing works.

So let's see what group borrowing can do, and then I'll explain how it works.

Group borrowing gives a program memory safety without run-time cost. 16

It catches use-after-free problems at compile time, and it does it in a way that has less restrictions than previous approaches.

Here's an example where a use-after-free error is caught at compile time:

It's an unusually flexible approach. Usually, compilers have trouble with the below program, but this approach understands that it's safe: 17

Group borrowing accepts a lot of patterns that are normally hard for borrow checkers, such as:

These are patterns we love from C++, but no language has figured out how to do all of these in a memory-safe way at compile time.

This quest led to a lot of interesting experiments with constraint references , linear types , reference counting , and a lot more .

My stance: if you want someone to take the time to read something, take the time to write it by hand.

Or more specifically, "can we make a borrow checker that supports multiple read-write borrow references to a single object?"

I'll explain this more below, but by "more complex data" I mean entire graphs of data, where objects can freely have references to other objects without restriction, like you see in C++, Java, etc. as opposed to something like Rust or Fortran where things generally can't have references to each other.

So when I say "read more complex data", I mean: how can we have immutable borrow references pointing at that kind of arbitrary graph of data?

(Note, Rust structs can have references to other Rust structs, but only temporarily. This is why ECS is such a popular choice in Rust games. That's why I still count Rust as more on the Fortran side of things.)

In short, this one is answered by Vale 's blend of generational references and region borrowing ; its immutable region borrowing lets the compiler track all pre-existing data as a temporarily frozen "region" of data, that we can have borrow references into.

For now, I'll just hint that Valen might have solved these by blending Vale 's approach, a certain thought experiment from 2023, Nick Smith's Group Borrowing approach, and a few twists to make things work together harmoniously.

Specifically, in today's compiler, one needs to manually dereference, index into arrays directly like my_vec.data[0] instead of the struct, and put types on all parameters like entity &Entity in world.entities[] .

This post you're reading right now is a much better explanation of group borrowing, but you can see the old post at Group Borrowing: Zero-Cost Memory Safety with Fewer Restrictions .

Soon I'll be writing an article on how all of these languages' approaches work and compare with each other, stay tuned!

It rejects less code by using first class permissions to merge lifetimes with the type checker. Definitely check it out!

Zeta's borrow checker can prove when two references point to different parts of the same data (they're "disjoint"). For example, it can prove list.get_mut(i) and list.get_mut(j) are disjoint when it knows that i != j , even if both indices are runtime values. Read more here !

Their syntax is still mostly the same, but Valen might change to be more of a "simpler Rust" syntactically.

I often called this conflict "the language killer" because it destroyed many versions of many experimental languages, including one of Vale's earlier approaches.

Between constraint references and Vale's current blend , there was an approach I called "hybrid-generational memory", where you could keep a reference alive by "tethering" a generational reference for the duration of a scope. I went through thirty two versions of it before giving up.

C++ wants this because that's often how we use it; we want a single unique_ptr owning an object, and a bunch of non-temporary raw pointers referring to it. Reference counting and garbage collection want the same sort of thing. In both cases, difficulties arise when someone else can modify an object while you have a borrow reference to it.

This can be a controversial goal; some of us believe that a reference's referent should never change out from under you, but an ID's/index's referent should be able to (like in Rust). Others believe that that's too restrictive. I think the user should be able to choose.

Though it's debatable if any language can get memory safety with zero run-time cost. See Chasing the Myth of Zero-Overhead Memory Safety , it applies to group borrowing as well.

Normally, borrow checkers don't understand how to have two references that can both modify an object, so they give compile errors . Group borrowing is flexible enough to not forbid these multiple read-write references, because it knows how to more precisely guard against use-after-free problems specifically.

For an example of this, see the "fn attack" examples in this page . This is usually hard for borrow checkers. Though, GhostCell sometimes helps!

Normal borrow checkers usually have trouble with this because the user wants two read-write references (which violates shared-xor-mutable): one to use directly, and one that lives inside the ScopeGuard object.

This could also be the foundation for a user-defined defer statement!

I don't have an example of this handy, but imagine that you wanted a bunch of File objects to each have a reference to a common FileSystem object. Borrow checking usually has problems with that (too many read-write references to the same object), but it should work fine in group borrowing.

I'll cover it more below, but using group borrowing as a starting point, we can:

For example, here's a step function that takes in a World reference, and a reference to one of the entities inside it.

The important part is the entity in world.entities[] mut , which I'll explain below.

Put together: entity is a reference to one of world 's entities 's elements, and we can modify it.

This is the core concept of the approach: the compiler knows where a reference points to, 25 because the user specifies (via in ) where it points to.

Now let's see how this looks in other languages, to see why this is so nice. (Or jump to how it works !)

Of course, the above requires care to uphold memory safety, since C++ doesn't check for memory safety at compile time.

Let's see an equivalent in Rust, where we do get automatic memory safety: 26

Rust is generally nice to work with, but in some cases (like this one), it isn't quite as fast or simple as the C++ case, because we need to re-fetch the reference every time someone needed a &mut to something else in the same hierarchy.

items.title: Homes and bridges swept away as fresh floods hit Nepal
items.summary: Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit less than two months ago, leaving thousands dead and missing.
items.content:
A major river in Nepal has flooded, sweeping away houses, bridges and damaging a part of hydropower station, authorities have said.

Around 50 people have been rescued from along the bank of the Budhi Gandaki River in the central Gorkha district, the army confirmed. No casualties have been reported yet, however five people are missing.

A video of the flood shows the moment raging waters sweep down a valley and wash away an entire building complex.

Nepal is on high alert and still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit its border towns with Tibet two months ago, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing.

Sunday's flood tore through the Gorkha district as children and communities prepared to mark the first day of the Dashain festival, a major moment in the Nepali calendar.

Families have been forced to flee their homes, with many facing uncertainty over where they will find safe shelter and access to essential supplies.

The flood swept away about a dozen houses and several suspension bridges, while a hydroelectric project was damaged, carrying some of the construction equipment away, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.

Within a couple of hours, the river's water levels at one location had risen from two metres (6ft 5in) to nearly 8.5m (27ft 9in), officials said.

Binod Parajuli, a meteorologist who works with the Nepalese government, said: "Our hydrological station was swept away and we are not getting any data from that location."

However, experts say the debris-flow is much smaller and travelled more slowly than the devastating flash floods in August.

What caused the latest flood is still unclear. Some say a landslide may have blocked the river or its tributary for some time, causing the dammed water to burst out, while others say locals upstream saw an ice-avalanche.

Save the Children is mobilising an emergency team to respond to Sunday's flood.

"Children's lives have been ripped apart in an instant yet again", the charity's director in Nepal, Tara Chettry, said.

"We are yet to see the full scale of the damage, but they may have lost their homes, schools and communities. Many children in Gorkha will still be in shock and distress after the mega floods in August, barely having a chance to get back on their feet."

The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli river, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused the previous disaster.

Many Nepalis swept away in the floods aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo

Hold ⌥ Space in any app and just talk. BetterWispr drops the ums and false starts, spells names your way and writes in the style you set for each app. Speech stays on your Mac.

Built in models transcribe your speech on your Mac, with no account and no cloud fallback. Models download once, then work offline.

Hold ⌥ Space while you speak and let go to finish. Switch to press to toggle, or record any shortcut with ⌘, ⌥ or ⌃, or an F key.

Nine built in models from Apple speech, Parakeet and Whisper. Parakeet covers English, Japanese and 25 European languages, and Whisper covers more. Or choose your own Sarvam AI, Smallest AI or OpenAI compatible API.

hey are you around for dinner tonight? let's do 7 if that works for you

Light, the default, drops English ums, repeats and false starts. Medium also edits for clarity with your notes model, on your Mac with Apple Intelligence or Ollama. None keeps every word.

Say comma, question mark or new paragraph as you talk. Say scratch that to delete the last sentence. Works in English.

The text lands in the app you were using. If paste is blocked, it is copied to your clipboard so nothing is lost.

Dictations stay on your Mac with the raw and the corrected text. Use Original brings back exactly what you said, and history turns off whenever you like.

See how many words you have spoken, your pace, the words cleanup saved you, which apps you dictate into and your daily streak. All of it is counted from history on your Mac.

New versions arrive from GitHub Releases through Sparkle and install only when their EdDSA signature matches.

Apache 2.0 licensed. Read every line on GitHub, report an issue, or build it yourself with make dev.

Install BetterWispr and follow the welcome guide through permissions and your first local speech model.

Place your cursor in a text field. Hold Option + Space and say what you want to write.

Let go to transcribe. Clean text arrives in the app you were using, in the style you set for it.

Models run on your Mac. Downloads happen when you choose to install them. Your speech doesn’t need a round trip to a transcription server.

There’s more than one good dictation app. Our comparisons cover local processing, offline use and writing workflows, with official sources.

Multilingual dictation, remembered corrections and voice editing.

Local speech recognition with optional AI writing enhancement.

Yes, once a compatible local model and its required assets are installed. Downloadable models need an explicit installation first. Apple on device speech also depends on supported languages and OS assets. There is no cloud transcription fallback.

Microphone permission lets BetterWispr record your voice. Accessibility permission allows automatic insertion into another app. Apple speech also requires Speech Recognition permission. You control these in System Settings.

BetterWispr checks the target app before inserting text. If it cannot safely paste, retrieve the transcript from the dashboard and copy it yourself. Secure fields and some apps may block automatic insertion.

Language support depends on the selected model. Parakeet TDT v3 covers 25 European languages, Parakeet Japanese covers Japanese, and Whisper offers broader multilingual recognition.
